This rebound aligns with a softening in Baltic rates earlier in the year, which are now improving alongside utilisation. The gains have been driven by increased activity on the Brazil-China and Transpacific routes. | Despite temporary disruptions from cyclones and flooding in early 2025, Australia’s miners maintained robust iron ore exports, with nearly 85% of shipments heading to China which supported Spot rates on the Brazil-China route to surge 27% MoM in 2H25.

commentary_title: Atlantic weakness offsets Pacific demand in Capesize market
commentary_summary: The Capesize segment weakened during the week, with tonne-miles index falling slightly WoW to 95.6, while Baltic C5TC rates fell in tandem. commentary_title: Softer Capesize freight market despite resilient Iron ore trade
commentary_summary: The Capesize market softened in Week 29, with utilisation declining to around 92%, along with the C5TC declining to $33,653. While the vessel fixing activity remained healthy, particularly in the Pacific, the available fleet increased across both basins, preventing cargo demand from sustaining the stronger momentum seen in previous weeks. | The Pacific remained active, with all major miners in the market, but rates declined as cargo volumes were insufficient to absorb the growing availability of vessels. In the Atlantic, the North Atlantic fleet list continued to increase, limiting activity and weighing on freight levels despite stable cargo demand. In contrast, the South Atlantic remained relatively resilient, with the C3 Brazil-China route rising above $33/tonne. | Rio Tinto's 2Q26 Pilbara iron ore sales exceeded market expectations, with first-half shipments rising YoY, pointing towards expectations of stronger Australian export volumes in the 2H26. Although higher diesel prices linked to Middle East tensions have increased mining costs, continued iron ore exports from Australia are expected to provide support for Capesize tonne-mile demand in the coming months.

commentary_title: Pacific correction offsets the resilient Atlantic region in Capesize market
commentary_summary: The Capesize utilisation fell to 92.1% following a 12% decline in Baltic benchmark C5TC rates over the last two weeks. The Pacific region was the main source of weakness as Chinese ports reopened following Typhoon Dolphin, allowing previously stuck vessels to return to the market. With vessel availability increasing faster than cargo demand, spot rates on Australia-China C5 fell sharply from above $16/tonne to around $14/tonne by the end of the week. | The reopening of Chinese ports released vessels delayed by Typhoon Dolphin, easing Pacific congestion and increasing available tonnage. Greater vessel availability intensified competition for cargoes, with some owners increasingly ballasting toward the Atlantic, where C3 remained more stable. This is likely to keep Pacific rates under pressure in the near term, while slower speeds and repositioning flows may support Atlantic availability. | South Brazil and West Africa–China routes continued to provide support, with C3 holding around $36/tonne having fewer ballasting vessels, and healthy first-half September demand helped offset softer sentiment elsewhere.

commentary_title: Strong demand meets tighter effective supply in the Capesize market
commentary_summary: The Drewry's Tonne-miles index for Capesize is on an uptrend, rising 2.8% WoW, reaching 98 in week 37. C5TC faced some correction WoW as the early-week Pacific rally lost momentum. C5 (Australia-China), however, remained firm, supported by strong miner participation and healthy demand for vessels. The willingness of miners to cover multiple vessels has kept the market well supported. | North China port closures due to strong winds and ongoing operational disruptions have delayed vessel schedules and reduced fleet efficiency. At the same time, higher bunker prices are encouraging owners to factor in higher fuel costs in voyage economics. | C3 levels (Brazil-China route) held around $41–42 per tonne, supported by limited available vessels and fresh October demand, with owners maintaining firm offers. However, elevated freight rates are increasingly challenging the economics of commodities. This could limit further upside if Atlantic demand softens, although the relatively short vessel list continues to put a cap.
